paragraphs.heading: A name from the underworld
paragraphs.text: The Hadean is an eon of Earth's history, and the Archean eon came after it. It is named after Hades, the Greek god of the underworld, a reference to the hellish conditions on early Earth. The planet had just formed, and scientists think its surface was molten lava. The American geologist Preston Cloud coined the term, originally as a label for the time before the earliest known rocks on Earth. The collision that created the Moon happened early in this eon.

paragraphs.heading: A thick early atmosphere
paragraphs.text: In the early Hadean, Earth had a very thick atmosphere, made mostly of water vapor, methane and ammonia. Its makeup likely resembled that of the gas giants. Volcanic outgassing and asteroid bombardments eventually changed it into an atmosphere rich in nitrogen and carbon dioxide.

paragraphs.heading: An ocean under pressure
paragraphs.text: As the surface cooled, water vapor in the atmosphere condensed into liquid water. Eventually a superocean formed that covered nearly all of the planet. Under the initial heavy atmosphere, the surface temperature was 230 °C and the pressure was above 27 standard atmospheres. Oceans of liquid water existed in spite of that heat, because water stays liquid at a pressure of 27 atmospheres. The most likely source of the ocean's water was outgassing from Earth's mantle. It is unlikely that bombardment delivered a substantial amount of it, because the isotope fractions of Earth and of comets are incompatible.

paragraphs.heading: Impacts that boiled the sea
paragraphs.text: During the Hadean, and on into the Archean, asteroid impacts would have disrupted the ocean from time to time. The geological record from 3.2 Ga holds evidence of several impacts by objects up to 100 kilometres across. A single impact of that kind would have boiled away as much as 100 metres of a global ocean and, for a time, raised the atmospheric temperature to 500 °C. How often meteorites struck is still under study, and there may have been long stretches when Earth could have liquid oceans and life.

paragraphs.heading: The few rocks that remain
paragraphs.text: Hadean rocks are very rare. They consist largely of zircon grains from one place, the Jack Hills in Western Australia. The oldest dated zircon crystals there date to 4.404 ± 0.008 Ga. That zircon is a slight outlier, and the oldest zircon with consistent dates is nearer 4.35 Ga, about 200 million years after Earth is thought to have formed. Zircon studies have found that there may have been liquid water between 4.0 and 4.4 Ga. In 2015, rocks in Western Australia that are 4.1 billion years old yielded traces of carbon minerals, which were interpreted as "remains of biotic life".

paragraphs.heading: Had the plates started moving
paragraphs.text: Plate tectonics may have started in the Hadean, but this is still uncertain. In 2008, a zircon study reported minerals in Australian Hadean rock that point to plate tectonics existing as early as 4 Ga, roughly 600 million years after Earth formed. Some geologists, however, suggest that meteorite impacts could have formed the zircons. The direct evidence is limited, because the zircons are largely gathered from one locality in Australia. Convection in the mantle was likely vigorous in the Hadean, but whether it led to plate tectonics or stayed confined under a rigid lid is still debated.
